claims.claim: There is a debate in cognitive science between those who argue that rapid physical inferences are computed by pattern recognition versus those who argue for mental simulation.
claims.source: A parallel debate is raging in cognitive science (Lerer et al., 2016; Conwell et al., 2019; Battaglia et al., 2013; Firestone and Scholl, 2017; Firestone and Scholl, 2016; Ludwin-Peery et al., 2019; Davis and Marcus, 2015; Chater and Oaksford, 2017; Davis et al., 2017; Ludwin-Peery et al., 2020), between those who argue that because human physical inferences occur rapidly (Firestone and Scholl, 2017) and preattentively (Firestone and Scholl, 2017) they are computed by something like a pattern recognition process, versus those who argue that human and primate physical inference behavior is best accounted for by mental simulation (Battaglia et al., 2013; Ullman et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2016; Gerstenberg et al., 2017; Rajalingham et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies representing different positions in the debate.

claims.claim: Visual information represented in the ventral visual cortex is used by the Physics Network for efficient inference of physical properties.
claims.source: We therefore hypothesize that visual information represented in the ventral visual cortex is used by the Physics Network for efficient inference of physical properties (see Almeida et al., 2013; Kravitz et al., 2011 for the cases of tool processing and visuospatial reasoning)
claims.evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the current findings and citations to related prior work.

claims.claim: An integrated computational model has been proposed that uses visual representations from a deep-learning-based inverse graphics model to initialize simulations in a physics-engine-based generative model.
claims.source: This idea has been recently proposed as an integrated computational model that uses visual representations from a deep-learning-based inverse graphics model to initialize simulations in a physics-engine-based generative model of object dynamics, which then can be used to perceive, predict, reason about, and plan with physical objects (Yildirim et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior computational modeling work.

claims.claim: Models with flexible, object-centric representations and the ability to learn from realistic visual inputs should be able to make predictions of physical stability on realistic stimuli.
claims.source: This class of models with flexible, object-centric representations and the ability to learn from realistic visual inputs (Bear, 2020; Mrowca, 2018) should be able to make predictions of physical stability on the realistic stimuli used in our experiment and also form the basis for neurally mappable encoding models of the candidate physics regions.
claims.evidence: The claim is a prediction based on inference from model properties and citations to relevant computational work.

claims.claim: The question of how an integrated vision-physics model is instantiated in the brain remains unanswered.
claims.source: The question of how such a model is instantiated, if at all, in the brain remains unanswered and provides a fertile avenue for future exploration.
claims.evidence: The claim is a statement about the current state of knowledge and future research directions.

claims.claim: Our mental physics engine may compress rich visual details into a relatively small number of individual objects and associated events for efficient approximation.
claims.source: According to one hypothesis, our mental physics engine compresses the rich details in our visual world into a relatively small number of individual objects and associated events in order to efficiently generate a reasonable approximation of the scene at the spatial and temporal scales relevant to human perception and action (Ullman et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is a hypothesis supported by citation to prior theoretical work.

claims.claim: Abstractions in mental physics may enable us to run simulations faster than real time with compressed timescales (like hippocampal replay).
claims.source: These abstractions may also enable us to run simulations faster than real time with compressed timescales (like hippocampal replay, Lee and Wilson, 2002), enabling us to make rapid and accurate predictions of the consequences of multiple actions under consideration, including our ability to make fast and automatic physical inference (Firestone and Scholl, 2017; Firestone and Scholl, 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on analogy to hippocampal replay and citations to relevant work.

results.result: ImageNet-trained CNNs (ResNet-50 and VGG-16) can classify physical stability within individual scenarios (60.1-75% accuracy) but fail to generalize across different scenarios (near-chance performance in cross-scenario tests). This demonstrates that CNN features do not carry abstract, generalizable information about physical stability.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 provide converging evidence from multiple CNN architectures showing within-scenario classification success but cross-scenario failure. The bootstrap statistical tests (p < 0.05 within, p > 0.15 across) and replication across two networks strengthen the conclusion. However, the study only tests two CNN architectures and one training dataset (ImageNet).

results.result: VTC contains scenario-specific information about physical stability for Physical-Objects and Physical-People scenarios but not for Animals-People scenarios, as demonstrated by significantly higher within-condition than between-condition pattern correlations with a significant interaction between scenario type and stability information (F1,12 = 72.2, p = 0.000002).
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10 provide consistent multivoxel pattern analysis results showing selective representation of physical (but not animate) stability in VTC. The statistical tests are appropriate and the interaction effect confirms the specificity. The n=13 sample size is modest but typical for fMRI studies.

results.result: The Physics Network contains scenario-specific information about physical stability for Physical-Objects and Physical-People scenarios but not for Animals-People scenarios, with a significant interaction between scenario type and stability information (F1,12 = 22.9, p = 0.0004).
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C14 parallel the VTC findings but in the Physics Network. The pattern analysis methodology is sound and the interaction effect confirms scenario-specificity. This result alone does not distinguish the Physics Network from VTC in terms of abstraction.

results.result: The Physics Network, but not VTC, shows generalizable representations of physical stability across Physical-Objects and Physical-People scenarios, with significantly higher within-condition than between-condition pattern correlations across scenarios and a significant interaction between brain region and cross-scenario stability information (F1,12 = 6.29, p = 0.027).
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C17 provide the critical evidence for abstract stability representation in the Physics Network. The cross-scenario pattern correlation analysis is well-designed and the region × generalization interaction directly tests the key hypothesis. This is the central finding distinguishing the two brain systems.

results.result: Eye movement patterns and interestingness ratings show minimal differences between stable and unstable conditions that do not interact with scenario type, ruling out these factors as confounds for the observed brain activation differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C21 provide important control analyses, but the eye-tracking data were only collected from 6 of 13 subjects, limiting statistical power. While one significant effect was found (C18), the lack of interactions (C19, C21) supports the authors' interpretation. However, the interestingness ratings were collected from a separate group of subjects, which is a limitation.

results.result: The generalization of stability information across physical scenarios in the Physics Network does not differ significantly between hemispheres (F1,12 = 2.75, p = 0.12) or lobes (F1,12 = 0.24, p = 0.63).
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C23 provide anatomical specificity analyses showing distributed representation across the Physics Network. The non-significant interactions indicate the effect is not localized to specific subregions, though the text notes parietal regions showed stronger effects. These are appropriate control analyses.

results.result: Early visual regions V1 and LOC show significant stability decoding only within the Physical-Objects scenario but no cross-scenario generalization, with significant interactions when contrasted with the Physics Network (F1,12 = 6.31, p = 0.027 for V1; F1,12 = 5.63, p = 0.035 for LOC).
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 demonstrate that abstract stability representation is specific to the Physics Network and not a general property of visual cortex. The interaction analyses appropriately test regional specificity. This strengthens the main conclusion by ruling out alternative explanations.

results.result: The Physics Network shows significantly greater univariate responses to physically unstable than stable conditions in Physical-Objects (p = 0.02) and Physical-People (p = 0.04) scenarios but not in Animals-People scenarios (p = 0.66).
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30 provide univariate evidence consistent with the forward simulation hypothesis. The selective response to physical (not animate) instability parallels the pattern analysis results. However, the authors acknowledge this is only preliminary evidence for simulation, as higher activity could reflect other processes.

results.result: The univariate response difference between unstable and stable conditions in the Physics Network shows significant interactions with lobe (parietal vs. frontal) for both Physical-Objects (F1,12 = 8.28, p = 0.014) and Physical-People (F1,12 = 8.53, p = 0.013) scenarios, and significant interactions with visual regions (V1, VTC, LOC) across scenarios.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C35 provide anatomical specificity for the univariate effects, showing they are stronger in parietal than frontal regions and specific to the Physics Network versus visual regions. The multiple interaction analyses appropriately test regional specificity, though post-hoc analyses would benefit from correction for multiple comparisons.

results.result: Visual motion area MT shows significantly higher univariate responses to unstable/perilous than stable/safe scenes across all three scenario types without showing significant stability information in multivoxel pattern activations.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C37 demonstrate that MT responds to predicted motion regardless of whether it is physical or animate, distinguishing it from the Physics Network. The dissociation between univariate and pattern responses is interesting but the interpretation regarding predicted versus implied motion requires further validation.

results.result: Images were selected such that stability classification accuracy on early CNN features (pool_1 from VGG-16) was near chance both within scenarios (42.9-53.6%) and across scenarios (41.1-51.8%), controlling for low-level visual feature confounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C65 describe an important stimulus control procedure to minimize low-level visual confounds. The near-chance performance on early CNN layers suggests the stimuli were well-controlled, though this approach assumes early CNN layers capture all relevant low-level features, which may not be fully accurate.

results.result: The fMRI experiment included 13 right-handed participants with normal vision who performed a physics localizer task and four runs of the main stability experiment with carefully controlled stimulus presentation and task design, though the study was cut short due to COVID-19.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C72 and C101 provide methodological details that are clearly stated and appropriate for the study design. The sample size of n=13 is modest but acceptable for fMRI studies with within-subject designs. The COVID-19 interruption is transparently reported.

results.result: Brain regions of interest were defined using a combination of group-level parcellation (derived from 27 subjects) and individual functional localizers with appropriate statistical thresholds (p < 0.001 uncorrected), with two occipital parcels excluded based on prior findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C82 describe a rigorous ROI definition procedure combining group constraints with individual localization. The use of uncorrected p < 0.001 is standard for ROI definition in fMRI. However, the exclusion of occipital parcels based on prior findings could introduce bias if those regions actually contain relevant information.

results.result: The study employed standard fMRI data acquisition and preprocessing methods, including appropriate scanner parameters, software tools (FreeSurfer, MATLAB), and analysis procedures (motion correction, GLM with nuisance regressors, pattern correlation analysis across even/odd runs).
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C73-C75, C83, and C103-C107 describe standard and appropriate fMRI methods. The even/odd run split for pattern analysis is a good practice to avoid temporal drift confounds. Eye-tracking was only available for 6 subjects, which is a limitation but transparently reported.

results.result: Prior work has established that CNNs trained on ImageNet support multiple visual tasks and have been claimed to predict stability, that the ventral pathway is well-modeled by such CNNs, and that frontoparietal regions are engaged in physical inference, though CNNs have only been tested in narrow domains and there is debate about whether stability judgments require simulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C48, C54-C55 accurately summarize relevant prior literature with appropriate citations. The characterization of the debate between pattern recognition and simulation accounts is fair and well-documented. These claims provide essential context for the current study.

results.result: The authors hypothesize that abstract physical stability representation requires forward simulation rather than pattern classification, predicting that the Physics Network rather than VTC would contain such representations, and that unstable scenes would evoke higher responses due to greater simulation demands.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52 and C56-C58 present clear, testable hypotheses logically derived from prior work and computational considerations. The reasoning connecting simulation demands to neural activity is plausible though not definitive. These hypotheses appropriately guide the experimental design and analyses.

results.result: The observed MT activation for predicted motion extends prior findings on implied motion, and the Physics Network findings are consistent with prior work showing these regions are engaged in physical tasks, represent physical concepts and mass, and overlap with action and tool use regions, though they also overlap with the multiple demand system.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C91 appropriately contextualize the current findings within prior literature. The distinction between implied and predicted motion (C85) is interesting but would benefit from direct experimental comparison. The acknowledgment that the Physics Network overlaps with multiple demand regions (C91) is an important caveat.

results.result: The authors discuss how their findings relate to ongoing debates about pattern recognition versus simulation in physical inference, propose that VTC provides input to the Physics Network for simulation-based inference, and suggest that mental physics may involve compressed representations enabling fast simulation, though many questions remain about implementation.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C100 present reasonable interpretations and hypotheses based on the data, but many are speculative (C95, C97, C99, C100). The proposed integration of ventral visual input with Physics Network simulation (C95) is plausible but not directly tested. The discussion appropriately acknowledges limitations and open questions (C98).

results.result: The interestingness rating validation showed that subjects rated high arousal IAPS images as more interesting than low arousal images (p < 0.000005), and the study received appropriate ethical approval from MIT.
results.evaluation: Claims C66 and C102 provide methodological validation and ethical compliance information. The IAPS validation (C66) supports the use of interestingness ratings as a proxy for attention, though this is an indirect measure. Ethical approval is appropriately documented.

results.result: CNNs trained on ImageNet can classify physical stability within scenarios (60.1-75% accuracy) but fail to generalize across different scenarios, with near-chance cross-scenario performance. This pattern holds for both ResNet-50 and VGG-16 architectures.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised concerns about the interpretation of CNN performance (point 6), noting that the modest within-scenario accuracy (60%) makes it unclear whether poor generalization reflects fundamental limitations or simply inadequate overall performance. In the second round, reviewers stated this concern was 'not completely satisfactory' and that the paper conflates whether CNNs can discriminate stability with whether their representations are generalizable, requesting this be discussed as a limitation.

results.result: VTC contains information about physical stability for Physical-Object and Physical-People scenarios but not for Animals-People scenarios, with a significant interaction between scenario type and stability information (F1,12 = 72.2, p = 0.000002).
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledged the pattern analysis results, they raised concerns about alternative explanations including scene comprehension difficulty and implied motion (points 1-2). The second round review (point 2) specifically noted that inferring specificity from a null effect in Animals-People is insufficient without testing whether Physical conditions show significantly better decoding than Animals-People conditions, stating 'a null effect is not evidence for absence.'

results.result: The Physics Network contains information about physical stability for Physical-Object and Physical-People scenarios but not Animals-People scenarios, with a significant interaction (F1,12 = 22.9, p = 0.0004).
results.evaluation: Similar to VTC results, reviewers raised concerns about alternative explanations (points 1-2). The second round review (point 2) explicitly stated that the authors 'infer specificity from a null effect' in Animals-People but 'a null effect is not evidence for absence,' requesting statistical testing of whether Physical conditions show significantly better decoding than Animals-People to support specificity claims.

results.result: The Physics Network shows cross-scenario generalization of stability representations between Physical-Objects and Physical-People scenarios, while VTC does not, with a significant interaction between region and generalization (F1,12 = 6.29, p = 0.027).
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised concerns about whether this reflects physical stability specifically versus other factors like implied motion or scene comprehension difficulty (points 1-2). The crucial test for specificity (point 3) was noted as missing in the first review, and in the second round (point 2), reviewers stated the response 'did not fully address the issue raised' and requested an ANOVA testing whether generalization in Physical conditions is significantly larger than in Animals-People conditions.

results.result: The Physics Network shows significantly greater univariate response to unstable versus stable conditions in Physical-Objects (p=0.02) and Physical-People (p=0.04) scenarios, but not in Animals-People scenarios (p=0.66).
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised multiple concerns about interpretation. Point 1 suggested elevated activity might reflect scene comprehension difficulty rather than physical simulation. Point 2 questioned whether effects reflect implied motion rather than physical stability. Point 11 challenged the theoretical reasoning about why unstable scenes require more simulation than stable scenes. These alternative explanations were not fully resolved.

results.result: Eye movement measures showed minimal differences between stable and unstable conditions (only saccade amplitude in Physical-People, p=0.028), with no interaction with scenario type. Interestingness ratings were higher for unstable conditions across all scenarios (p<0.001) but did not interact with scenario type (p=0.23).
results.evaluation: Reviewers initially raised concerns about attention confounds (point 1) and requested behavioral data. The authors collected interestingness ratings and eye-tracking data to address these concerns. While reviewers questioned whether 'interestingness' was adequate (point 12), they did not reject these control analyses in subsequent reviews, and the data served to address the attention confound concern.

results.result: V1 and LOC show significant decoding of stability only in Physical-Objects scenarios but no cross-scenario generalization, with significant interactions when contrasted with the Physics Network (F1,12 = 6.31, p=0.027 for V1; F1,12 = 5.63, p=0.035 for LOC).
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged these control region analyses. Point 10 raised questions about specific patterns (negative generalization in V1, LOC generalization effects) but these were treated as requests for clarification rather than challenges to the findings. The interactions demonstrating differences between Physics Network and visual regions were not disputed.

results.result: Visual motion area MT shows significantly higher univariate responses for unstable/perilous scenes across all three scenario types, but no significant stability information in multivoxel patterns.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised concerns about whether Physics Network effects could be explained by implied motion (point 2), but the MT results showing responses across all scenarios including Animals-People were presented as evidence distinguishing motion sensitivity from physical stability processing. Reviewers did not challenge the MT findings themselves.

results.result: Within the Physics Network, stability effects show significant interactions with lobe (parietal vs. frontal) but not hemisphere, with parietal regions showing stronger effects for both Physical-Objects (F1,12=8.28, p=0.014) and Physical-People (F1,12=8.53, p=0.013) scenarios.
results.evaluation: These subregion analyses were not specifically challenged by reviewers. They were presented as additional characterization of the Physics Network and reviewers did not raise concerns about these findings in their comments.

results.result: Univariate stability effects in the Physics Network are significantly stronger than in visual regions (V1, VTC, LOC), with significant region × stability interactions for Physical-Objects and Physical-People scenarios.
results.evaluation: These comparisons between Physics Network and visual regions were not challenged by reviewers. They serve as control analyses demonstrating regional specificity and were accepted as supporting evidence for the main claims.

results.result: Methodological details including participant characteristics (13 subjects, all right-handed), stimulus parameters (14 images per condition, 8° visual angle), and experimental design (physics localizer, 4 runs of main experiment with 1-back task).
results.evaluation: Reviewers requested more stimulus examples (point 13) and clarification of design choices (points 5, 9) but did not challenge the basic methodological approach. The experimental design was described as using 'cleverly designed stimuli' and 'well-crafted experiments' in the public review.

results.result: Stimuli were selected such that early CNN layer features (pool_1 from VGG-16) showed near-chance classification accuracy both within scenarios (42.9-53.6%) and across scenarios (41.1-51.8%).
results.evaluation: This stimulus selection procedure was not challenged by reviewers. It represents a methodological control to ensure low-level visual features did not trivially distinguish stable from unstable conditions.

results.result: fROI definition procedures using physics localizer (physics > color contrast, p<0.001) and visual localizers, with group-level parcels derived from 27 subjects and individualized using group-constrained subject-specific methods.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the fROI definition methods. Point 4 requested better contextualization relative to prior work (Fischer et al., 2016; Schwettmann et al., 2019) that used similar methods, but did not question the validity of the approach.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate CNN performance claims (C1-C5). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting converging evidence and statistical rigor but limited architectures tested. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN, raising concerns that modest within-scenario accuracy (60%) makes poor generalization ambiguous and that the paper conflates discrimination ability with generalizability.

Both evaluate VTC pattern analysis (C7-C10). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, finding appropriate statistical tests and specific interaction effects. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN, arguing that inferring specificity from null effects in Animals-People is insufficient without direct statistical comparison showing Physical conditions significantly outperform Animals-People.

Both evaluate Physics Network pattern analysis (C11-C14). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with sound methodology. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN with identical concerns as VTC: inferring specificity from null effects is inadequate and requires statistical testing showing Physical conditions significantly better than Animals-People.

Both evaluate cross-scenario generalization (C15-C17). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, calling this the critical evidence for abstract stability representation. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN, questioning whether effects reflect physical stability versus alternative explanations (implied motion, scene comprehension) and requesting ANOVA testing whether Physical generalization significantly exceeds Animals-People.

Both evaluate control analyses for attention confounds (C18-C21). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN due to limited eye-tracking sample (6/13 subjects) and separate group for interestingness ratings. Peer review rates SUPPORTED, acknowledging these analyses addressed attention concerns despite questioning whether 'interestingness' was optimal.

Both evaluate univariate instability effects (C28-C30). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED as consistent with simulation hypothesis but acknowledges preliminary nature. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN, raising multiple alternative explanations: scene comprehension difficulty, implied motion, and questioning theoretical reasoning about why unstable scenes require more simulation.

Both evaluate regional specificity analyses (C24-C27). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting appropriate interaction analyses ruling out alternative explanations. Peer review rates SUPPORTED, acknowledging control region analyses with only minor clarification requests about specific patterns.

Both evaluate MT motion sensitivity (C36-C37). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting interesting dissociation between univariate and pattern responses but requiring validation. Peer review rates SUPPORTED, accepting MT findings as evidence distinguishing motion sensitivity from physical stability processing.

Both evaluate anatomical specificity within Physics Network (C22-C23 in OpenEval; C22-C23, C31-C32 in peer review). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED for distributed representation analyses. Peer review rates SUPPORTED, treating these as accepted characterization of Physics Network subregions.

Both evaluate regional comparisons (C31-C35 in OpenEval; C33-C35 in peer review). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED for parietal-frontal differences and Physics Network versus visual region specificity. Peer review rates SUPPORTED, accepting these as control analyses demonstrating regional specificity.

Both evaluate stimulus control procedure using CNN layers (C63-C65). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting near-chance early layer performance suggests good control but acknowledges assumption limitations. Peer review rates SUPPORTED, accepting this as valid methodological control for low-level visual features.

Both evaluate fROI definition methods (C76-C82). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting rigorous procedure but potential bias from excluding occipital parcels. Peer review rates SUPPORTED, requesting better contextualization relative to prior work but not challenging validity.

Both evaluate general methodological details (C59-C62, C67-C72 in OpenEval; C6, C59-C62, C67, C69-C72 in peer review). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with appropriate methods and transparent reporting. Peer review rates SUPPORTED, describing 'cleverly designed stimuli' and 'well-crafted experiments' with requests for clarification but no fundamental challenges.

Partial overlap on methodological claims. OpenEval R14 covers C6, C73-C75, C83, C103-C107 (standard fMRI methods, eye-tracking limitations) rated SUPPORTED. Peer review R11 covers broader experimental design including C6, accepting methods despite requesting more stimulus examples.

OpenEval evaluated literature review claims (C38-C48, C54-C55) as SUPPORTED, finding accurate summaries and fair characterization of theoretical debates. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval evaluated hypothesis formulation claims (C49-C52, C56-C58) as SUPPORTED, finding clear testable hypotheses logically derived from prior work. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval evaluated contextualization claims (C84-C91) as SUPPORTED, noting appropriate framing within prior literature and important caveats about Physics Network overlap with multiple demand regions. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval evaluated interpretation and speculation claims (C92-C100) as UNCERTAIN, noting many are speculative (integration of ventral visual input, future directions) but appropriately acknowledge limitations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval evaluated methodological validation and ethics claims (C66, C102) as SUPPORTED, noting IAPS validation for interestingness ratings and appropriate ethical documentation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
